🐣 Start from zero · Step 4 of 5 · 5 min

How learning works: you and the machine

Why you forget, and how to make knowledge stay.

🧠 Your brain learns from examples too

You did not learn what a dog is from a rule. You saw many dogs, and someone said “dog” each time. Your brain found the pattern.

A model learns in a similar way: from examples and from its mistakes. So what helps you learn is worth knowing, and it is also how this site is built.

📉 Why you forget

New knowledge fades fast. Without a reminder, much of what you read today will be hard to recall in a week.

This is normal: the brain lets go of what it does not use. The trick is to use it at the right moments.

Task. You want to remember a lesson for a long time. What works best?

Show the answer

Right answer: Close the page and try to recall the main ideas

Pulling an answer out of your memory makes the memory stronger. Rereading and highlighting feel good, but they do much less. That is why this site keeps asking you questions.

🗓️ Come back at the right time

The best moment to recall something is just before you would forget it. After each successful recall the memory lasts longer, so the breaks can grow.

This is called spaced repetition. The memory check on this site does it for you: after each right answer a question comes back after a longer break. A wrong answer brings it back the next day.

1 day → 2 days → 4 days → 8 days → …

Task. You answer a card right every time. It came back after 1, 2, 4 and 8 days. After how many days will it come back next?

Show the solution

The breaks double: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16. A handful of short checks keeps an idea for months.

Task. In the memory check you answer a card wrong. When does it come back?

Show the answer

Right answer: Tomorrow

A wrong answer sends the card back to the first box. It returns the next day, so you can fix it while it is fresh.

🗣️ Explain it to someone

If you can explain an idea in your own simple words, you understand it. If you get stuck, you have found the exact place to read again.

On this site it is called “Explain it back”: after a lesson you write two or three sentences and compare them with the lesson's key ideas.

Task. Does it build a strong memory, or does it only feel like learning?

Show the solution

Recall it, explain it, space it out. The other three are comfortable, and that is the problem: the brain does little work.

Task. You and a model learn in similar ways. Find the pairs.

Show the solution

One big difference: you understand what things mean. A model only finds patterns in numbers.

Task. What is spaced repetition?

Show the answer

Right answer: Coming back to an idea after longer and longer breaks

You recall the idea just before you would forget it, and each time the break grows: 1, 2, 4, 8 days and more.

Task. Which is the best sign that you really understand an idea?

Show the answer

Right answer: You can explain it in your own simple words

Familiar is not the same as known. Explaining it shows the gaps at once.

Remember

  • You and a model both learn from examples and from mistakes.
  • Recalling from memory beats rereading.
  • Spaced repetition: come back after 1, 2, 4, 8 … days, just before you would forget.
  • Explaining in your own words shows what you really know.

Tasks with hints, a memory check that brings the idea back before you forget it, and your progress. Free, no sign-up.
